lead: A state equation gives the slope of the state vector at every instant. To predict the state later, we need a closed-form map from the present state and past input to the future state. That map is the state transition matrix Φ(t)=e<sup>At</sup>. It is used to simulate circuits, motors and drones, to check stability, and to design observers and state feedback. The same formula also turns a matrix differential equation into an ordinary convolution.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.1 for state models, Laplace transforms from mathematics, and see Unit 2, Time Response Analysis, for first-order and second-order responses.

blocks.text: The state equation is x′(t) = A x(t) + B u(t). Here x is the n×1 state vector, x′ is its time derivative, u is the m×1 input vector, A is the n×n system matrix and B is the n×m input matrix. The initial state is x(0). The equation is linear, so its solution splits into two parts: the part caused by x(0) with u = 0, and the part caused by u with x(0) = 0.

The zero-input part is Φ(t)x(0). Φ(t) is the n×n state transition matrix. It carries the state from time 0 to time t when no input is present. The zero-state part is a convolution of the input with the same matrix: ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>t</sup> Φ(t−τ)B u(τ)dτ. τ is a dummy time variable. B u(τ) is the input vector mapped into state space.
x(t) = Φ(t)x(0) + ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>t</sup> Φ(t − τ) B u(τ) dτ
blocks.where: x(t) is the n×1 state at time t; Φ(t)=e<sup>At</sup> is the n×n state transition matrix; x(0) is the initial state; B is the n×m input matrix; u(τ) is the m×1 input at time τ; τ is the integration variable.

blocks.text: For a single-input system B is n×1. For a free system u=0, so x(t)=Φ(t)x(0). If x(0)=0, only the convolution remains. This split is why the matrix exponential is the central object of state-space analysis.

Take the Laplace transform of x′=Ax+Bu term by term. Let X(s) be the transform of x(t) and U(s) the transform of u(t). The derivative rule gives sX(s)−x(0)=A X(s)+B U(s). Collect X(s): (sI−A)X(s)=x(0)+B U(s). I is the n×n identity matrix. Therefore X(s)=(sI−A)<sup>−1</sup>x(0)+(sI−A)<sup>−1</sup>B U(s).

The matrix (sI−A)<sup>−1</sup> is called the resolvent. Its inverse Laplace transform is Φ(t). So Φ(t)=L<sup>−1</sup>[(sI−A)<sup>−1</sup>]. Compare the transformed solution with the time-domain formula. The first term gives Φ(t)x(0). The second term gives the convolution, because a product in the s-domain is a convolution in time. This is the standard route for a 2×2 or 3×3 model.

blocks.where: Φ(t) is the state transition matrix; A is the system matrix; I is the identity matrix; L<sup>−1</sup> means inverse Laplace transform; s is the Laplace variable.

blocks.text: For a 2×2 matrix A, compute sI−A, its determinant Δ(s), and the inverse. Δ(s) is the characteristic polynomial. Its roots are the eigenvalues λ<sub>1</sub> and λ<sub>2</sub>. They are also the poles of the system. After inverse Laplace, each entry of Φ(t) is a sum of terms e<sup>λ<sub>1</sub>t</sup> and e<sup>λ<sub>2</sub>t</sup>. If a root repeats, a term t e<sup>λt</sup> appears.

items: Split each entry by partial fractions.
Take inverse Laplace to get Φ(t).

blocks.text: With distinct eigenvalues, an equivalent method is Φ(t)=M diag(e<sup>λ<sub>1</sub>t</sup>, e<sup>λ<sub>2</sub>t</sup>) M<sup>−1</sup>. M has eigenvectors of A as columns. The diagonal matrix holds the two modes. This is faster when eigenvectors are easy. Do not exponentiate A entry by entry: e<sup>At</sup> is a matrix defined by the series I+At+(At)²/2!+…, not by applying e<sup>at</sup> to each element.

Some syllabi also use the Cayley–Hamilton series: for 2×2, e<sup>At</sup>=α<sub>0</sub>(t)I+α<sub>1</sub>(t)A; find α<sub>0</sub>, α<sub>1</sub> from the eigenvalues. Only a few universities teach this in detail.

figure.caption: The state equation is mapped through the resolvent to Φ(t); the response adds the initial-state term and the input convolution. Notice that Φ(t) feeds only the sum, and the input enters through the convolution.

spec.title: State solution
spec.aria: The state equation is transformed to find Φ(t); the response sums the initial-state term and the input convolution.

examples.question: For A = [[0, 1], [−2, −3]], find Φ(t). Then find x(t) for u = 0 and x(0) = [1; 0]. Give the state at t = 0.5 s.
steps: With u=0, the solution is x(t)=Φ(t)x(0). Form sI−A = [[s, −1], [2, s+3]].
The determinant is s(s+3)+2 = s²+3s+2 = (s+1)(s+2). The eigenvalues are −1 and −2.
examples.check:
import math
t = 0.5
e1 = math.exp(-t)
e2 = math.exp(-2*t)
phi11 = 2*e1 - e2
phi12 = e1 - e2
phi21 = -2*e1 + 2*e2
phi22 = -e1 + 2*e2
x1 = phi11
x2 = phi21
for v in (phi11, phi12, phi21, phi22, x1, x2):
    print(f"{v:.10f}")

traps: e<sup>At</sup> is not found by taking e to each entry of A. Use (sI−A)<sup>−1</sup> or eigenvalues.
Sign slip in sI−A: diagonal entries are s−a<sub>ii</sub>, off-diagonal entries are −a<sub>ij</sub>. A missed minus changes the determinant.
Do not mix zero-input and zero-state: Φ(t)x(0) uses the initial state; the convolution uses the input. Setting u=0 removes the convolution, not Φ(t)x(0).
Φ(0)=I, not A and not the zero matrix. Check every computed Φ(t) at t=0.
For repeated eigenvalues, simple e<sup>λt</sup> terms may not be enough; a t e<sup>λt</sup> term can appear.

quiz.q: Why does the state solution have two terms?
quiz.a: The system is linear, so superposition holds. One term is the zero-input response from x(0); the other is the zero-state response from u.

quiz.q: For A = [[0, 1], [−2, −3]], what eigenvalues and modes appear in Φ(t)?
quiz.a: Eigenvalues are −1 and −2. The modes are e<sup>−t</sup> and e<sup>−2t</sup>; no repeated root means no t e<sup>−t</sup> term.

quiz.q: If Φ(t)=[[e<sup>−t</sup>, 0], [0, e<sup>−2t</sup>]] and x(0)=[3; −1], find x(t) for u=0.
Why is e<sup>At</sup> not computed element by element?
quiz.a: e<sup>At</sup> is defined by the matrix series I+At+(At)²/2!+…. Matrix multiplication couples entries, so off-diagonal terms appear even when A has zeros. Elementwise exponentiation misses that coupling.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, matrix exponentials are computed by scaling and squaring with Padé approximations, not by Laplace inversion. Control software uses them for sampled-data models, where Φ(T) and ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>T</sup>Φ(T−τ)B dτ are discretised. Robotics uses the same idea for linearised motion models. Search next: matrix exponential, resolvent, discretisation of state-space models, Van Loan method.
